observations.content:
## Overview
Quantum Mechanics is the fundamental branch of [[Physics]] that provides a mathematical description of the physical properties of nature at the scale of [[Atoms]] and subatomic particles. It is the foundation of all quantum physics, including quantum chemistry, [[Quantum Field Theory]], and quantum technology. Unlike [[Classical Mechanics]], which describes the motion of macroscopic objects using deterministic laws, quantum mechanics operates in a realm where energy, momentum, and other quantities are often restricted to discrete values, a process known as quantization.

## Details
At its core, quantum mechanics replaces the classical notion of definite paths with the concept of the [[Wave Function]], a mathematical entity that provides information about the probability amplitude of a particle's position, momentum, and other physical properties. The evolution of this function over time is governed by the [[Schrödinger Equation]]. 

One of the most defining characteristics of the quantum world is the role of the observer. In classical physics, measuring a system does not change its state. In quantum mechanics, however, the act of measurement causes the wave function to 'collapse' from a [[Superposition]] of several possible states into a single, definite state. This probabilistic nature suggests that the universe is not deterministic at its most fundamental level, a concept that continues to spark philosophical debate among scientists.

## History
The development of quantum mechanics began in the late 19th and early 20th centuries as classical physics failed to explain several experimental observations. 

### Early Developments
In 1900, [[Max Planck]] proposed that energy is emitted or absorbed in discrete units called 'quanta' to explain [[Black-body Radiation]]. This was a radical departure from the continuous energy flow assumed in classical theories. In 1905, [[Albert Einstein]] extended this idea by suggesting that light itself is quantized into particles called [[Photons]], which successfully explained the photoelectric effect.

### The Quantum Revolution
The 1920s saw the rapid formalization of the field. [[Niels Bohr]] introduced a model of the atom where electrons occupy fixed orbits, and [[Louis de Broglie]] proposed that all matter exhibits wave-like properties, a concept known as wave-particle duality. Between 1925 and 1927, [[Werner Heisenberg]] developed matrix mechanics, and [[Erwin Schrödinger]] formulated wave mechanics. These two frameworks were later proven to be mathematically equivalent, providing the robust theoretical structure used today.

## Features
### Wave-Particle Duality
This principle states that every particle or quantum entity may be described as either a particle or a wave. The [[Double-slit Experiment]] famously demonstrates this by showing that electrons create interference patterns (like waves) but arrive at a detector as discrete points (like particles).

### Uncertainty Principle
Formulated by Werner Heisenberg, the [[Uncertainty Principle]] asserts that there is a fundamental limit to the precision with which certain pairs of physical properties, such as position and momentum, can be known simultaneously. The more precisely one is measured, the less precisely the other can be predicted.

### Quantum Entanglement
[[Quantum Entanglement]] occurs when particles interact in such a way that the quantum state of each particle cannot be described independently of the state of the others, even when separated by large distances. This leads to correlations that defy classical logic, famously termed 'spooky action at a distance' by Einstein.

## Impact and Applications
Quantum mechanics is not merely a theoretical framework; it is the basis for much of our modern world. The understanding of quantum states in [[Semiconductors]] led to the invention of the [[Transistor]], the fundamental building block of all modern computers and smartphones. 

In the field of medicine, [[Magnetic Resonance Imaging]] (MRI) utilizes the quantum property of nuclear spin to create detailed images of the human body. The development of the [[Laser]] is another direct application of quantum principles involving stimulated emission. Looking toward the future, [[Quantum Computing]] aims to harness superposition and entanglement to perform computations that are currently impossible for classical supercomputers, potentially revolutionizing fields like cryptography and material science.

## Overview

Quantum mechanics is a fundamental theory in physics that provides a detailed description of the physical properties of nature at the scale of [[atoms]] and subatomic particles. It is the foundation of all quantum physics, including quantum chemistry, [[quantum field theory]], quantum technology, and quantum information science. Unlike classical physics, which relies on deterministic laws to describe macroscopic objects, quantum mechanics introduces a probabilistic framework where energy, momentum, and other quantities are often restricted to discrete values, a process known as quantization.

At its core, quantum mechanics reveals that the universe at a microscopic level operates under principles that often defy human intuition. It explains why atoms are stable, how light interacts with matter, and the underlying mechanisms of electricity and magnetism at the smallest scales. The transition from classical mechanics to quantum mechanics at the beginning of the 20th century marked a paradigm shift in science, fundamentally changing our understanding of reality and leading to the development of much of our modern technology.

## Details

The mathematical framework of quantum mechanics is built upon the concept of the [[wave function]], usually denoted by the Greek letter psi (Ψ). The wave function is a mathematical description of the quantum state of a system and provides the probability amplitude for the position, momentum, and other physical properties of particles. According to the Born rule, the square of the magnitude of the wave function represents the probability density of finding a particle in a specific location upon measurement.

One of the most striking features of quantum theory is the [[Uncertainty Principle]], formulated by [[Werner Heisenberg]]. It states that certain pairs of physical properties, such as position and momentum, cannot be simultaneously known with arbitrary precision. The more accurately one property is measured, the less accurately the other can be known. This is not a limitation of measurement instruments but a fundamental property of the universe itself. Furthermore, quantum systems exhibit [[superposition]], meaning they can exist in multiple states at once until an external observation or measurement causes the system to 'collapse' into a single definite state.

## History

### Early Development

The roots of quantum mechanics lie in the late 19th-century failures of classical physics to explain certain phenomena. In 1900, [[Max Planck]] proposed that energy is radiated and absorbed in discrete 'packets' or [[quanta]] to solve the black-body radiation problem, specifically the ultraviolet catastrophe. In 1905, [[Albert Einstein]] extended this idea by suggesting that light itself consists of individual particles, later called photons, to explain the photoelectric effect. 

### The Golden Age of Quantum Physics

During the 1920s, the theory underwent rapid development. [[Niels Bohr]] introduced a model of the atom where electrons occupy fixed orbits, and transitions between these orbits result in the emission or absorption of specific frequencies of light. However, the true breakthrough came with the formulation of matrix mechanics by [[Werner Heisenberg]] and wave mechanics by [[Erwin Schrödinger]]. These two distinct mathematical approaches were later shown to be equivalent. In 1927, the [[Copenhagen interpretation]] became the dominant philosophical view of the field, emphasizing the role of the observer and the probabilistic nature of quantum events.

## Features and Principles

### Wave-Particle Duality

Quantum entities like electrons and photons exhibit both wave-like and particle-like behaviors depending on the experiment being performed. This is famously demonstrated in the [[double-slit experiment]], where single particles create an interference pattern characteristic of waves when not observed, but behave like discrete bullets when their path is tracked.

### Quantum Entanglement

[[Quantum Entanglement]] is a phenomenon where two or more particles become linked in such a way that the state of one particle cannot be described independently of the others, even when separated by vast distances. A change in the state of one entangled particle appears to instantaneously affect the state of the other, a concept [[Albert Einstein]] famously critiqued as 'spooky action at a distance.'

### Quantization

In classical systems, properties like energy can take any continuous value. In quantum systems, many physical quantities are 'quantized,' meaning they can only take specific, discrete values. This is evident in the energy levels of an [[atom]], where electrons must reside in specific shells rather than anywhere in between.

## Impact and Applications

The implications of quantum mechanics extend far beyond theoretical physics. It is the basis for the development of the [[transistor]], which powers every computer, smartphone, and electronic device today. [[Lasers]], which utilize stimulated emission to produce coherent light, are another direct application of quantum principles. In medicine, Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) relies on the quantum spin of atomic nuclei.

Looking toward the future, the field of [[Quantum Computing]] seeks to use superposition and entanglement to perform calculations at speeds unreachable by classical supercomputers. Additionally, [[Quantum Cryptography]] offers the possibility of perfectly secure communication channels that are immune to eavesdropping. The study of [[Particle Physics]] also relies heavily on quantum mechanics to understand the [[Standard Model]] and the fundamental forces of the universe.

## 개요

양자역학은 분자, 원자, 전자, 소립자와 같은 미시적인 대상의 물리적 현상을 설명하는 [[현대 물리학]]의 한 분야이다. 19세기 말까지의 물리학인 [[고전 역학]]이 거시적인 물체의 운동을 완벽하게 설명했다면, 양자역학은 에너지가 연속적이지 않고 특정한 단위로 떨어져 있다는 '양자'의 개념을 도입하여 미시 세계의 불규칙하고 확률적인 거동을 설명한다. 오늘날 양자역학은 반도체, 레이저, 핵물리학 등 현대 기술의 근간을 이루고 있으며, 우주의 근본 원리를 이해하는 데 필수적인 이론으로 자리 잡았다.

## 상세

양자역학의 가장 본질적인 특징은 대상이 입자와 파동의 성질을 동시에 지닌다는 [[파동-입자 이중성]]에 있다. 고전 역학에서는 물체의 위치와 운동량을 정확히 측정할 수 있다고 가정하지만, 양자역학에서는 [[베르너 하이젠베르크]]가 제안한 [[불확정성 원리]]에 의해 두 물리량을 동시에 정확히 아는 것이 불가능하다. 이는 측정 기술의 한계가 아니라 자연의 근본적인 성질로 받아들여진다.

시스템의 상태는 '파동 함수'라는 수학적 도구로 기술되며, 이는 입자가 특정 위치에서 발견될 확률 밀도를 나타낸다. [[에르빈 슈뢰딩거]]가 고안한 슈뢰딩거 방정식은 시간이 지남에 따라 이 파동 함수가 어떻게 변화하는지를 설명한다. 관측이 이루어지기 전까지 입자는 여러 상태가 겹쳐 있는 [[양자 중첩]] 상태에 있으며, 관측되는 순간 하나의 상태로 결정된다는 [[코펜하겐 해석]]이 가장 널리 받아들여지고 있다.

## 역사

양자역학의 태동은 1900년 [[막스 플랑크]]의 흑체 복사 연구에서 시작되었다. 플랑크는 에너지가 연속적이지 않고 특정한 최소 단위인 '양자'의 정수배로 존재한다는 가설을 세웠다. 이후 1905년 [[알베르트 아인슈타인]]이 [[광전효과]]를 설명하기 위해 빛이 입자(광자)의 성질을 가진다는 광양자설을 발표하며 이 이론은 더욱 발전하였다.

1913년 [[닐스 보어]]는 원자 내 전자의 궤도가 양자화되어 있다는 보어 모형을 제시하였으며, 1920년대 중반에 이르러 하이젠베르크의 행렬 역학과 슈뢰딩거의 파동 역학이 등장하며 현대적인 양자역학의 체계가 완성되었다. 이후 [[폴 디랙]] 등에 의해 상대성 이론과 결합하여 [[양자 전기 역학]]과 [[표준 모형]]으로 확장되었다.

## 주요 원리

### 양자 중첩
하나의 양자 체계가 측정되기 전까지는 가능한 여러 상태를 동시에 가질 수 있다는 원리이다. 이는 [[슈뢰딩거의 고양이]]라는 유명한 사고 실험으로 잘 알려져 있다.

### 양자 얽힘
둘 이상의 입자가 서로 연결되어, 하나의 상태가 결정되는 순간 아무리 멀리 떨어져 있어도 다른 입자의 상태가 즉각적으로 결정되는 현상이다. 아인슈타인은 이를 '유령 같은 원격 작용'이라 부르며 회의적이었으나, 이후 실험을 통해 실재함이 증명되었다.

### 양자 터널링
입자가 고전적으로는 통과할 수 없는 에너지 장벽을 확률적으로 통과하는 현상이다. 이는 태양의 핵융합 반응이나 현대의 플래시 메모리 작동 원리에 핵심적인 역할을 한다.

## 응용 및 의의

양자역학은 현대 문명의 거의 모든 전자 기기에 적용된다. [[반도체]] 소자의 설계는 전자의 양자역학적 거동을 이해하지 않고는 불가능하며, [[레이저]]는 원자의 에너지 준위 전이를 이용한 대표적인 양자 장치이다. 또한, 자기공명영상([[MRI]]) 장비는 원자핵의 스핀 성질을 이용한다.

미래 기술로는 양자 중첩과 얽힘을 이용해 기존 슈퍼컴퓨터의 한계를 뛰어넘는 연산 능력을 제공할 [[양자 컴퓨터]]와 도청이 불가능한 [[양자 암호]] 통신이 활발히 연구되고 있다. 양자역학은 단순히 기술적 도구를 넘어, 인간이 자연을 인식하는 철학적 패러다임에도 큰 변화를 가져왔다.
